delete.title: Delete log(s)
delete.label: Delete
delete.confirm: Are you sure you want to delete the selected log(s)?

help.intro: This is the record of who changed what. Every create, update, delete, restore and status move on a tracked entity writes a row as it happens — nothing on this screen writes one, and nothing can edit one.
help.step_1_title: Read a row as entity plus id
help.step_1_body: An id is only meaningful inside its entity: id 5 exists for a user, a product and an order alike. Filtering by entity alone is fine; filtering by id alone is not, and the two together are what follow one record through its life.
help.step_2_body: The acting account is linked, and the name is also stored on the row as it read at the time — so renaming or deleting that account later does not rewrite history. Source tells you whether the change came from a request, a scheduled job or a seed.
help.step_3_body: The request id is shared by everything a single request changed, which is how a cascade is read: one delete that took a subtree with it shows up as many rows under one id. A bulk operation also shares its timestamp, stamped once for the whole set.
help.step_4_body: Details is whatever the operation chose to record — the fields that moved, the ids that went down together. It is per action rather than a fixed shape, so it is shown as stored.
help.step_5_body: Every filter here matches exactly and there is no free-text search: entity, entity id, action, request id, source, and a recorded-date range. Delete takes the rows you select, several at a time, and is final — there is no deleted state to restore from.
help.note: Nothing prunes this table on a schedule, unlike the log, so it grows for as long as the application runs. It is also the only place a past change is recorded: purge it for space, never to tidy up, and keep enough to answer who changed a record and when.
